en: The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Imperially Appointed Court Honorable Official, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, Dharma-bhadra, in compliance with the Imperial Edict.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—all of whom were elders within the Dharma, great arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, completely severed the fetters of existence, and realized liberation—such a multitude numbering one thousand people.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to this thought:
"I should now go to the place of the sacred stupa in the Bamboo Grove Mountains.
Having formed this thought, he went to that place together with the assembly of bhikṣus; having arrived there, he entered the rains retreat within it.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, together with a full thousand senior great Arhats, was dwelling at the site of the Spirit Tower on Mount Daṇḍaka.

At that time, the King, reflecting on his desire to go and hear the Dharma, immediately ordered the preparation of his carriage, making it more magnificent than usual. There were twelve thousand chariots in the procession, eighteen thousand beds with exquisite garments and precious vessels, and the eight musical instruments and four divisions of the army led the way and followed behind, as he traveled surrounded by his kinsmen, ministers, and attendants.

At that time, the king departed from the city for Mount Daṇḍaka, proceeding to the Buddha’s dwelling to attend upon and make offerings to him; there were also brahmins and householders who followed the king to the Buddha’s presence.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing the king approach, manifested five signs—namely, the sign of the crown protuberance, the sign of the parasol, the sign of the mani-jewel, the sign of the fly-whisk, and the sign of the precious sword—to adorn his Buddha-body.

At that time, having arrived at the Buddha’s assembly, the Great King removed the marks of royal sovereignty. He approached the Buddha, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms toward the Buddha. With wondrous words he praised the Buddha’s virtues; then, having prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet, he circumambulated him three times and stood before the Buddha.
Addressing the World-Honored One by his own name, he said: “I am King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha.”
He spoke again, saying:
"I am King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha.
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha replied three times:
"So it is, so it is. You are King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha."
Furthermore, with gentle words, he comforted the king and invited him to take his seat.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the king rejoiced and leaped for joy, then withdrew to sit to one side.

The king’s retinue and ministers likewise knelt before the Buddha with palms joined, praised the Buddha’s virtues with exquisite speech, and after prostrating their heads at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side.

Among the various brahmins and householders, some praised him with words and prostrated; some merely joined their palms and bowed their heads in worship; and some gazed at the Buddha from afar in silence. These various groups each sat to one side.
At that time, the brahmins, elders, and others in the assembly suddenly saw the venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa standing in attendance by the Buddha’s side, and they thought to themselves:
"Alas, the venerable Uruvilvā Kāśya, the elder, now practices the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa!"
The World-Honored One, knowing that those brahmins and householders had conceived doubts in their minds, immediately spoke a verse to ask Kāśyapa:
“You, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, In the past, tended the sacrificial fire without interruption;
For what benefit did you see it? What dharma did you obtain?”
"Please explain this meaning to me quickly.
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa replied with a verse:
"All flavors of food and drink in the world, Even the sensual pleasures that people delight in,"
"Seeing this benefit, I sought it with resolve; therefore, I have tended the fire without interruption.
The Buddha spoke again in verse, asking Kāśyapa:
"How could one be so attached to the pleasures of desire, even to the point of craving the flavors of food and drink?"
"O you whose heart is cherished by humans and devas, please explain this meaning to me quickly.
The Venerable Kāśyapa replied in verse:
"Because I did not understand the supreme state of tranquility, I fell into despondency."
Devoted solely to the five desires and lacking correct reasoning, they thus attend to the sacrificial fire without interruption.
Claiming that through the Vedas and fire-worship one realizes liberation, sentient beings are thereby deluded in mind;
like the blind, they are no different from the dead, having fallen away from the state of supreme tranquility.
I now behold the true unconditioned dharma, well-expounded by the Great Naga, the Supreme Teacher;
for the sake of great benefit, the Muni, the World-Honored One of Great Diligence, has appeared in the world.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
“Kāśyapa! Welcome;
you dwell well, free from all perverse thoughts, and are well able to discern the most supreme Dharma.”
“Kāśyapa! You should now skillfully transform this assembly.

Thereupon, the Venerable Kāśyapa, having received the Buddha’s command, immediately entered *samādhi* and manifested great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). He vanished from the midst of the assembly and appeared in the eastern sky, manifesting the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—and even displaying the fire-samādhi.
From within the fire element, he emits various kinds of light—namely blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of crystal;

furthermore, water issues from his upper body while fire issues from his lower body, and water issues from his lower body while fire issues from his upper body, appearing and disappearing in a continuous, uninterrupted succession.

In this same manner, in the southern, western, and northern directions, within the midst of space, he likewise manifested the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—and even entered the fire samādhi, emitting various kinds of light from within the element of fire, namely blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of crystal;

furthermore, water issued from his upper body while fire issued from his lower body, and fire issued from his lower body while water issued from his upper body, appearing and disappearing in an uninterrupted succession.

At that time, after the Venerable Kāśyapa had manifested his supernormal powers in the empty space of the four directions, he withdrew those powers, approached the Buddha, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One, my Teacher!
"I am a great śrāvaka.
He spoke again, saying:
"O my Teacher, the World-Honored One!"
"I am a great śrāvaka.
The Buddha replied to Kāśyapa,
saying, "I am your teacher!"
“You are a great śrāvaka.
He replied again, “I am your teacher!”
"You are a great śrāvaka;
you may return to your seat.
At that time, the brahmins, elders, and others in the assembly again thought to themselves:
"Is it that even this venerable elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is still practicing the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa, the Buddha?
Knowing his thoughts, the Buddha addressed King Bimbisāra, saying: "Great King!"

One should know that form has arising and cessation; having understood that this form has arising and cessation, one should likewise know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also arise and cease, and that these aggregates of phenomena have arising, which is to say they have cessation.
"Great King!

Regarding this dharma of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), if a son of good family can truly understand that what arises is immediately extinguished and that the aggregate of form is fundamentally empty—since the aggregate of form is empty, arising is not truly arising; since there is no arising, what is there to be extinguished?"
As it is with the aggregate of form, so it is with all the aggregates.
If a son of good family, having understood this, realizes that the aggregates are neither born nor extinguished, neither abiding nor proceeding, then there is no self.
"I say that such a person shall be one of true tranquility for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
At that time, the various brahmins, elders, and others in the assembly had this thought:
"By what dharma can one come to know that there is no self, and no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?"
What are those things called "self," "other," "person," "sentient being," or "life-span"?

Furthermore, what are these categories such as the "controller" (maṇava), the "agent," the "procreator," the "ariser," the "unmoving one," the "speaker," the "discriminator," and the "knower"? Which among them is not born and which does not perish?
"Furthermore, for what reason do those beings experience the karmic results of the wholesome and unwholesome deeds they have performed?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts that had arisen in the minds of those brahmins and householders, addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!"
If one speaks of a self when there is no self, this is the mark of a selfhood belonging to the ignorant, unlearned, ordinary worldling.

Bhikṣus, you should know that "I" is fundamentally non-existent and there is no "I"; yet regarding these phenomena of suffering, if one conceives of them as arising, the aggregate of suffering arises; if one conceives of them as ceasing, the aggregate of suffering ceases.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), if one forms the perception of arising, conditioned phenomena arise; if one forms the perception of cessation, conditioned phenomena cease.
Conditioned phenomena are produced through these causes and conditions; by means of these conditions, there is both arising and ceasing.
Having thus understood, in accordance with reality, the nature of arising and ceasing, I am now able to speak to all sentient beings. Monks!

With the pure divine eye, which surpasses the fleshly eye, I see sentient beings—those who arise and cease, those who are beautiful or ugly, noble or base, high or low, those in happy or miserable realms—and I know, in accordance with reality, the wholesome and unwholesome karmas performed by sentient beings and the retributions they receive.

Furthermore, sentient beings possess the three unwholesome karmas of body, speech, and mind; they slander the noble ones and give rise to false views. Due to these false views, they perform various unwholesome actions and practice various unwholesome dharmas. By reason of these causes and conditions, after their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and undergo the sufferings of hell.

Furthermore, when sentient beings possess the goodness of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, they do not slander the noble ones and give rise to right view. By virtue of this right view, they perform various wholesome karmas and practice various wholesome dharmas. Due to these causes and conditions, after the end of their lives, they are reborn in the celestial realms as devas.
“Monks, I know things as they truly are; I see things as they truly are.

At that time, I did not say that there is a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-principle. Furthermore, regarding those such as the ‘knower’—where do they arise and where do they cease? They perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds and experience their retribution. In phenomena such as these, there is no notion of a self; it is because of the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) that the five aggregates exist, and it is by virtue of that notion of phenomena that the five aggregates arise.”

Furthermore, monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; when volitional formations arise, the arising of phenomena occurs. When volitional formations cease, the cessation of phenomena is attained. Monks!

Thus, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) exists because its causes have accumulated; through the cessation of that accumulation, the suffering of conditioned formations ceases. Once the phenomena of suffering have ceased, all non-dharmas (unwholesome states) also cease and no longer arise again; such is the ultimate limit of the exhaustion of the phenomena of suffering.
"Monks! What is the realization of cessation?
This very end of suffering is true quiescence; it is the attainment of coolness; it is called the ultimate exhaustion."

"O Bhikṣus! This is the phrase for tranquility: namely, the relinquishing of all phenomena; when craving for phenomena is exhausted and desire for phenomena is extinguished, this is precisely tranquil Nirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
What do you think?"
"Is form permanent or impermanent?
The king replied,
"The cessation of form is precisely its impermanence."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Is this suffering, or is it not suffering?
The King replied:
“World-Honored One!
The cessation of suffering is not itself suffering; that which is suffering is a perverted dharma.
This perverted dharma—”
“Is it those śrāvakas of little knowledge and little learning who claim, ‘I am a great śrāvaka,’ or ‘I possess great wisdom,’ and thus give rise to this notion of self and the notion of others?”
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
The King replied,
"When they cease, they are impermanent."
The Buddha asked,
"Is this suffering, or is it not suffering?
The King replied:
"Suffering arises from inversion; this dharma of inversion is itself suffering.

"Is it because those śrāvakas, possessing little knowledge and little learning, give rise to the notion of a self—that they therefore claim, 'I am a great śrāvaka,' or 'I am one of great wisdom'—that they harbor this notion of a self?"
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Great King! It is so, it is so!

Reflect upon this well: regarding this dharma of the aggregate of form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; near or far—all such dharmas are from the very beginning non-existent, signless, and without self.”
"Great King!
By means of that right knowledge, you should see things as they truly are.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:

“Great King! Even regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; near or far—all such phenomena are from the very beginning non-existent, signless, and without self.”
"Great King! It is so.
One should see it as it truly is through that right wisdom."

At that time, having heard this Dharma, the assembly of śrāvakas and others realized the impermanence of form, and likewise realized the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Consequently, they gave rise to revulsion and detachment; through revulsion and detachment, they immediately attained liberation. Having realized liberation, right knowledge became manifest before them: "I have attained liberation; my births are exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not undergo further existence."
At that time, when King Bimbisāra heard this Dharma being taught, his vision of the Dharma became pure, free from dust and devoid of defilement;

furthermore, within the assembly, eighty thousand devas and humans, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of brahmins and householders, likewise attained the purity of the vision of the Dharma, free from dust and devoid of defilement.

At that time, King Bimbisāra’s Dharma-eye became pure; he attained right knowledge and vision, dwelt firmly in the Dharma, was freed from all desires and all suffering and affliction, and attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma within the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, the Great King rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and with sincere faith, prostrated himself before him, saying to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I have attained great benefit! I have attained great benefit!

I vow to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and receive the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*); from this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from killing and so on, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants.
He spoke again, saying:

"I now respectfully entreat the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to return to the city of Rājagṛha. I pray only that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept my invitation; for as long as this life lasts, I shall serve and provide offerings, including clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all articles of daily use, providing them in full abundance. This shall likewise apply to the entire community of bhikṣus."
At that time, having accepted the King’s invitation, the World-Honored One remained silent.
Seeing that the Buddha had granted his consent by remaining silent, the Great King prostrated himself with his head to the ground, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew.
The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra Spoken by the Buddha
